content: This review is an update of previous evaluations of eslicarbazepine acetate (ESL) as an add-on therapy for drug-resistant focal epilepsy, originally published in 2011 and last updated in 2017. While most individuals with epilepsy respond well to treatment, approximately 30% continue to experience seizures despite the use of multiple antiepileptic drug regimens. This review specifically examines the efficacy and tolerability of ESL in this population. For this update, a comprehensive search was conducted on September 10, 2020, using databases such as the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web) and MEDLINE (Ovid). The search included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials from sources like CENTRAL, PubMed, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). No language restrictions were applied. Reference lists of retrieved studies were reviewed, and manufacturers of ESL, as well as field experts, were contacted for information on unpublished or ongoing studies. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trials of ESL as an add-on therapy in individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Two independent reviewers selected studies for inclusion and extracted data. The primary outcomes assessed included a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency, seizure freedom, treatment withdrawal, adverse effects, and drug interactions. Analyses were conducted on an intention-to-treat (ITT) basis, and dose-response relationships were evaluated using regression models. Seven trials involving 2185 participants aged 2 to 77 years were included in the review. The studies were generally at low or unclear risk of bias, except for a high risk of attrition bias. All studies were funded by the pharmaceutical company BIAL. The overall risk ratio (RR) for achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency was 1.57 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.34 to 1.83). For adults, the RR was 1.71 (95% CI 1.42 to 2.05; 5 studies, 1799 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). For children aged 6 to 18 years, the RR was 1.35 (95% CI 0.98 to 1.87; 2 studies, 322 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Dose-response analysis indicated that higher doses of ESL were associated with greater reductions in seizure frequency. ESL was also associated with seizure freedom, with an RR of 3.16 (95% CI 1.73 to 5.78; 6 studies, 1922 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). However, participants receiving ESL were more likely to discontinue treatment due to adverse effects (RR 2.72, 95% CI 1.66 to 4.46; 7 studies, 2185 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). There was no significant increase in treatment withdrawal for any reason (RR 1.25, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.70; 7 studies, 2185 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Adverse effects associated with ESL included dizziness (RR 2.77, 99% CI 1.85 to 4.15), nausea (RR 2.55, 99% CI 1.39 to 4.67), somnolence (RR 1.75, 99% CI 1.18 to 2.61), diplopia (RR 4.07, 99% CI 1.86 to 8.89), and vomiting (RR 2.37, 99% CI 1.19 to 4.74). The overall certainty of the evidence was moderate, primarily due to the high rate of treatment discontinuation in studies involving adults. In conclusion, ESL is effective in reducing seizure frequency when used as an add-on therapy for adults with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The included trials were of short-term duration. While there is some evidence suggesting that ESL may also reduce seizure frequency in children aged 6 to 18 years, the results for this age group remain inconclusive.
